overviewTitle: When bathroom problems become a legal repair issue
overview: Bathrooms contain essential washing and sanitation facilities. A defect may justify legal review where the landlord is responsible, has been told about it and has not completed an effective repair within a reasonable time.
issues: A toilet, bath, shower or basin that cannot be safely used
Leaks from supply pipes, waste pipes, seals or fittings
Persistent bathroom mould linked to leaks, ventilation or building defects
Loose tiles, unsafe flooring, damaged surfaces or exposed electrics
duties: The landlord may be responsible for supplied sanitary installations, water and drainage pipework, the structure and other defects affecting safe use. Cosmetic wear alone is different from a defect that restricts an essential facility or causes continuing damage.
impact: Record whether the household lost access to its only toilet, bath or shower, whether water spread to other rooms and whether children, older people or disabled occupants were particularly affected.
faqs: What counts as bathroom disrepair?
Broken essential fittings, leaks, unsafe surfaces and related damp or electrical hazards may qualify when they fall within the landlord’s responsibility.
Can I claim if my toilet is broken?
Potentially, particularly where it is the only toilet and remains unusable after urgent notice. Eligibility depends on responsibility, response and evidence.
Is the landlord responsible for bathroom mould?
That depends on its cause. Evidence of leaks, inadequate extraction or another building defect can be important.

overviewTitle: No heating or hot water in a rented home
overview: A landlord-supplied boiler or fixed heating system should be maintained in working order. Complete failure, intermittent faults and repeated loss of hot water can all have a serious effect, especially in cold weather.
issues: A boiler that will not start, loses pressure or repeatedly cuts out
Radiators that remain cold because of a system defect
No hot water or unreliable hot-water supply
Unsafe noises, leaks, warning lights or recurring error codes
duties: Heating and hot-water installations commonly fall within the landlord’s repair duties. Response time depends on urgency, weather, vulnerability and what is required, but an emergency call-out or temporary measure does not remove the need for a lasting repair.
impact: Keep a day-by-day record of indoor conditions, hot-water loss and any temporary heaters supplied. Note additional electricity use and how cold conditions affected sleeping, washing, work, school or medically vulnerable occupants.
faqs: How quickly should heating be repaired?
There is no universal deadline, but loss of heating or hot water can require urgent action, particularly in winter or where occupants are vulnerable.
Can temporary heaters resolve the issue?
They may reduce immediate risk but do not necessarily amount to an effective repair of the landlord’s heating system.
Can additional energy costs be considered?
Reasonable additional electricity costs may be relevant when supported by bills, meter readings or receipts.

overview: Plaster can deteriorate because of damp, water ingress, movement or age. Falling material may create a direct safety risk, while repeated surface patching may hide an unresolved building defect.
issues: Bulging, cracked or hollow-sounding areas
Falling pieces above beds, stairs or living areas
Damage returning after patch repairs
Staining, salts or mould showing continuing moisture
duties: The landlord’s responsibility often turns on the cause. Where defective roofing, plumbing, brickwork or another repair issue damages the plaster, dealing only with the surface may not be enough.
impact: Record rooms or furniture that had to be moved, cleaning required after repeated falls, damage to possessions and any injury or near miss. Do not disturb an area that appears unstable merely to gather evidence.
faqs: Is crumbling plaster just wear and tear?
Minor cosmetic deterioration may be, but extensive, unsafe or moisture-damaged plaster can indicate actionable disrepair.
What if it keeps being patched?
Photograph every recurrence and keep appointment records. Repeated failure may show that the underlying cause has not been addressed.
Can damp-related plaster be included?
Yes, where the damp and resulting damage are connected to a defect for which the landlord is responsible.

overview: Condensation can contribute to mould, but recurring growth may also arise from leaks, defective roofs, penetrating damp, inadequate fixed ventilation, insulation faults or other problems with the building.
issues: Black mould returning after cleaning
Damp patches, peeling finishes or tide marks
Musty smells and mould behind furniture
Water penetration, condensation or inadequate extraction
duties: The correct cause must be investigated. A landlord may be responsible for relevant defects in the structure, installations or supplied ventilation, and should not dismiss a report without considering the condition of the property and household circumstances.
impact: Track every affected room and photograph conditions over time. Note damaged clothing, furniture and decoration, additional heating or cleaning, and any respiratory, skin or mental-health symptoms discussed with a clinician.
faqs: What if the landlord blames condensation?
Continue to ventilate and heat reasonably where possible, but ask for the building and any leaks or ventilation defects to be properly investigated.
Do I need medical evidence?
It is not required to prove that mould exists, but medical records can be important if compensation is sought for an effect on health.
Should I keep cleaning the mould?
Follow appropriate safety guidance and photograph it first. Cleaning may reduce exposure but does not resolve an underlying defect.

overview: Cracked, loose or eroded brickwork and failed pointing may allow water penetration, reduce weather resistance or indicate a structural concern requiring professional inspection.
issues: Loose bricks, open joints or badly eroded mortar
Cracks that widen, recur or pass through several courses
Bulging walls or unstable masonry
Internal damp corresponding with external defects
duties: The structure and exterior commonly fall within a landlord’s repair obligations. The cause and seriousness should be assessed by an appropriate professional rather than assumed from appearance alone.
impact: Photograph the same points over time without entering unsafe areas. Record falling debris, restricted access, internal water damage and any inspection, scaffold or temporary safety measures.
faqs: Are all cracks serious disrepair?
No. Hairline cosmetic cracking differs from movement or failing masonry, so professional assessment may be needed.
How should brickwork be reported?
Use the landlord’s repair channel, describe any immediate danger or water penetration and retain the report reference.
Can self-funded work be recovered?
Do not commission major structural work without advice. Recovery of costs depends on responsibility, necessity and the steps taken beforehand.

overview: Exposed conductors, overheating fittings and damaged cables can create shock or fire risk. Treat warning signs as a safety issue and use the landlord’s emergency reporting procedure.
issues: Exposed, frayed or visibly damaged wiring
Sparking, scorch marks or a burning smell
Sockets or switches that become unusually hot
Water entering near cables, lights or the consumer unit
duties: A landlord is generally responsible for the fixed electrical installation it supplies. Qualified inspection and testing may be necessary; tenants should not remove covers or attempt electrical repairs themselves.
impact: Note when circuits or rooms could not be used, any appliances damaged and any temporary loss of essential facilities. In an immediate emergency, prioritise safety and contact the appropriate emergency or electricity service.
faqs: How do I know if wiring is dangerous?
Visible damage, heat, sparks, burning smells, repeated trips and water contact are warning signs requiring prompt professional attention.
What if the landlord refuses to investigate?
Keep written records, repeat any urgent warning and seek advice about council enforcement and legal options.
Can damaged appliances be included?
Potentially, if evidence connects the damage to a defect for which the landlord was responsible.

overviewTitle: The effect of defective roofs and gutters
overview: Missing coverings, failed flashing, blocked or broken gutters and defective downpipes can lead to repeated water ingress, penetrating damp and deterioration inside the home.
issues: Leaks or staining that worsen during rainfall
Missing tiles, damaged coverings or failed flashing
Overflowing, detached or leaking guttering
Damp at ceilings, external walls or around chimney breasts
duties: Roofs, gutters and other external elements normally form part of the structure and exterior. A temporary patch may be reasonable initially, but continuing ingress should be investigated and repaired effectively.
impact: Film active leaks when safe, then photograph staining and damage after rain. Record affected electrics, ceilings, possessions and any drying, cleaning or room restrictions.
faqs: What if the leak only happens in heavy rain?
Report the pattern and provide dated videos. Intermittent weather-related ingress can still demonstrate an external defect.
Can damp caused by a roof leak be included?
Yes, the internal consequences and underlying roof defect should be considered together.
How long will a claim take?
Timescales vary with inspections, repairs, evidence and the landlord’s response; no fixed completion date can be promised.

overviewTitle: When defective sanitaryware may support a claim
overview: Toilets, baths, showers and basins are essential facilities. Serious breakage, instability, leakage or blockage can affect hygiene and safe daily use.
issues: A toilet that will not flush, leaks or is unstable
A cracked or unsafe bath, basin or shower tray
Waste connections causing repeated leaks or foul smells
Essential fittings remaining unusable after attempted repair
duties: Responsibility commonly covers landlord-provided sanitary installations and connected water or drainage systems. Tenant-caused damage and minor cosmetic defects are assessed differently.
impact: Record whether another facility was available, how long essential sanitation was lost, water damage to surrounding areas and reasonable additional costs caused by the failure.
faqs: What is defective sanitaryware?
It can include broken, unsafe, leaking or unusable toilets, basins, baths, showers and their connected fittings.
How urgent is a broken toilet?
Loss of the only toilet is likely to require an urgent response. Make the circumstances clear when reporting it.
What if a repair failed?
Report the recurrence immediately and preserve photographs and the details of the earlier attendance.

overviewTitle: What makes spray foam insulation defective?
overview: Spray foam is not automatically defective, but unsuitable material, poor installation or inadequate ventilation can contribute to condensation, trapped moisture or concern about roof timbers.
issues: Foam covering timbers so their condition cannot be checked
Condensation, moisture or timber deterioration
Inadequate roof ventilation after installation
Missing installation records, guarantees or suitability checks
duties: Responsibility depends heavily on who commissioned and installed the product and whether it caused a problem with the rented property. Independent expert evidence is particularly important.
impact: Keep installation documents, surveys and correspondence. Do not attempt removal yourself: it can damage the roof and disturb material, and responsibility for the cost should be considered before work begins.
faqs: Can I claim if the foam predates my tenancy?
Possibly, if the landlord is responsible for a resulting condition and failed to act after notice. The installation history still matters.
Is every spray-foam installation actionable?
No. A claim requires evidence of a defect, responsibility and resulting impact or loss.
What evidence is most useful?
Installation paperwork and an independent roof or building survey are often central.

overviewTitle: Common electrical faults in rented homes
overview: Repeated power loss, defective sockets and unsafe landlord-provided installations can disrupt essential facilities even where the wiring itself is not visibly exposed.
issues: Circuits repeatedly tripping without an obvious appliance cause
Dead, loose or intermittent sockets and switches
Lights flickering because of a fixed-installation fault
A defective landlord-supplied electrical appliance or extractor
duties: The landlord is generally responsible for keeping the fixed electrical installation safe and in repair. The precise cause should be diagnosed by a qualified person before liability is assumed.
impact: List each outage, circuit and affected facility. Keep electrician reports, appliance damage evidence and records showing loss of cooking, refrigeration, lighting or heating.
faqs: How is an electrical fault different from dangerous wiring?
A fault may involve performance or supply without visible wiring damage; both can require qualified investigation and may overlap.
Are landlord-provided appliances covered?
They may be, depending on the tenancy and the appliance supplied. Record its details and fault history.
How quickly should faults be addressed?
Urgency depends on safety and the facilities affected. Fire or shock risks require immediate reporting.

overviewTitle: Gas appliance faults and safety risks
overview: A faulty landlord-supplied boiler, fire or cooker can create safety risks and remove heating, hot water or cooking facilities. Suspected gas leaks must be treated as emergencies.
issues: A gas smell, warning alarm or suspected leak
An appliance condemned or isolated by an engineer
Incomplete combustion, soot or repeated shutdowns
Loss of heating, hot water or cooking from a supplied appliance
duties: Landlords have specific gas-safety duties as well as repair obligations. Appliances and flues must be checked by appropriately registered engineers; tenants should never attempt to reconnect an isolated appliance.
impact: For a suspected leak, leave the danger area and contact the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999. After safety is secured, retain engineer records, warning notices and evidence of lost facilities or additional costs.
faqs: How long can a landlord leave a gas leak?
A suspected leak is an emergency, not a routine repair. Contact the emergency service first and notify the landlord immediately.
What if an appliance is switched off as unsafe?
Keep the warning notice and record what essential services were lost and what alternatives were offered.
Can stress and disruption be considered?
The overall impact may be relevant, but any compensation depends on evidence, responsibility and the legal assessment.

overviewTitle: How flooding and water damage develop
overview: Flooding may result from pipes, drains, roofs, gutters, windows or communal systems. The source must be identified so the correct party and permanent repair can be established.
issues: Burst or leaking supply and waste pipes
Blocked drains, overflowing gutters or communal leaks
Roof, flashing, window or waterproofing failure
Recurring water entry after incomplete work
duties: The landlord may be responsible for relevant structure, exterior and installations, but liability depends on the source and notice. Emergency attendance should be followed by investigation of continuing damage, damp and mould.
impact: Prioritise electrical and personal safety. Photograph the water source and spread where safe, prepare an itemised list of damaged belongings, and keep drying, cleaning or temporary-accommodation receipts.
faqs: What if the water came from another flat?
Report it to your own landlord and provide everything known about the source. Responsibility may require investigation across properties.
Can belongings be included?
Potentially, when ownership, value, damage and legal responsibility are adequately evidenced.
Should I dispose of damaged items?
Photograph them thoroughly and retain proof of purchase where possible; ask your adviser or insurer before disposal if practical.

overviewTitle: When an insect infestation is linked to disrepair
overview: Cockroaches, bedbugs and other insects are not automatically the landlord’s responsibility. A claim may arise where building defects, drainage or communal conditions controlled by the landlord caused or prolonged the infestation.
issues: Gaps around pipes, walls, windows or external doors
Infestation spreading from communal or neighbouring areas
Drainage, refuse or damp conditions encouraging insects
Repeated treatment without proofing or structural work
duties: Evidence linking the insects to a repair or management failure is crucial. Pest-control reports can help distinguish structural entry routes from issues associated with a tenant’s own belongings or conduct.
impact: Record sightings, affected rooms and treatment dates. Keep reports identifying entry points and receipts for treatment, cleaning, contaminated food or damaged possessions.
faqs: How can I prove disrepair caused the infestation?
A pest controller’s observations, photographs of entry points and evidence of communal spread can be important.
What if the landlord blames me?
Preserve evidence of hygiene, reports and structural causes and ask for the allegation and inspection findings in writing.
Can pest-control costs be considered?
Reasonable costs may be relevant if the landlord was legally responsible and the expenditure was necessary and evidenced.

overviewTitle: When kitchen problems become a repair issue
overview: A kitchen needs safe facilities for preparing food, washing and using supplied services. Leaks, unsafe units, damaged worktops and defective installations can restrict normal use.
issues: Unstable wall units, cabinets or work surfaces
Leaks beneath sinks or from landlord-controlled plumbing
Unsafe sockets, wiring or supplied extraction
Damage preventing safe food preparation, washing or storage
duties: Responsibility depends on which fixtures were supplied, the tenancy and the cause. The landlord may be responsible for installations, structural defects and fittings it owns, while ordinary minor upkeep can remain with the tenant.
impact: Explain exactly which facilities could not be used and whether another cooking or washing area existed. Retain evidence of water damage and reasonable additional food, cleaning or appliance costs.
faqs: What counts as kitchen disrepair?
Serious defects can include unsafe supplied units, persistent leaks and failures affecting essential water, electrical or food-preparation facilities.
Can I claim if I cannot use the kitchen?
Loss of use is relevant, but the cause, duration, landlord’s response and evidence all require assessment.
Are faulty kitchen electrics included?
Fixed electrical faults may fall within landlord duties and should be reported urgently where there is a safety risk.

overviewTitle: Active leaks, plumbing and drainage failures
overview: Leaks and drainage failures can cause rapid water damage, sanitation problems and recurring damp. The immediate flow and the underlying defect both need attention.
issues: Leaking supply, heating or waste pipework
Blocked or backing-up landlord-controlled drains
Low pressure or loss of water caused by a defect
Repeated wastewater, foul smells or contamination
duties: Landlord duties commonly cover water, sanitation and drainage installations within their responsibility. The cause may sit inside the home, in a communal stack or beneath the building, so appropriate diagnosis matters.
impact: Report active water escape urgently and take reasonable steps to limit damage without putting yourself at risk. Keep plumber findings, water bills, cleaning costs and evidence of affected rooms and belongings.
faqs: How quickly must an active leak be repaired?
Response should reflect the urgency and potential damage. A major escape of water normally requires immediate reporting and prompt action.
What if the leak keeps returning?
Create a timeline of each incident and attendance; recurrence can show that the underlying cause remains.
Can increased water charges be included?
They may be relevant where bills or meter readings support a direct connection to the unresolved leak.

overview: Rotten boards, unstable surfaces, failed coverings and sudden level changes can create trip or collapse risks, especially when water damage has weakened the structure beneath.
issues: Loose, broken or collapsing floorboards
Rot or softness caused by continuing leaks
Raised, torn or insecure landlord-supplied covering
Holes, severe unevenness or unsupported areas
duties: Responsibility depends on whether the problem concerns the structure, landlord-supplied material or tenant-installed covering. The landlord should investigate reports suggesting structural weakness or an underlying leak.
impact: Mark off dangerous areas where possible and avoid testing unstable sections. Record restricted rooms, falls or near misses, damaged items and any need to relocate furniture or occupants.
faqs: Does worn carpet count?
Ordinary wear differs from a serious trip hazard or structural failure. Ownership, cause and severity matter.
What evidence supports a flooring claim?
Clear photographs, inspection findings, repair history and records of any injury or loss of room use.
What if it was already damaged when I moved in?
Inventory and check-in evidence can show the starting condition, but notice and the landlord’s later response still matter.

overviewTitle: Pest and vermin infestations caused by defects
overview: Rats and mice may enter through broken air bricks, gaps, damaged drains, service penetrations or communal areas. Eradication may fail unless the route of entry is repaired.
issues: Holes or gaps around pipes, walls and external doors
Broken drains, air bricks or communal refuse areas
Gnawing, droppings, nesting or contaminated food
Recurring activity after baiting or trapping
duties: The source determines responsibility. A landlord may need to repair structural access points and address communal causes, while the tenant should cooperate with treatment and reasonable hygiene advice.
impact: Use pest-control reports to identify likely entry routes. Keep photographs, treatment history, records of food or possessions discarded and details of rooms that became unsafe or unusable.
faqs: What if pest treatment did not work?
Treatment alone may fail where entry points remain. Report recurring activity and request proofing or structural investigation.
Can I claim if pests existed before I moved in?
Potentially, particularly where records show a pre-existing landlord-controlled cause and failure to remedy it.
How is compensation assessed?
Duration, severity, loss of use, evidenced costs and responsibility are considered individually; there is no fixed tariff.

overview: Windows and external doors should provide reasonable security, weather resistance and safe operation. Broken frames, seals, locks and glazing can affect several parts of daily life.
issues: Frames that are rotten, warped, loose or will not close
Broken locks, handles, hinges or external-door security
Water penetration or severe draughts through defects
Failed glazing, unsafe panes or unusable ventilation
duties: The structure and exterior generally include external windows and doors, although responsibility for damage and minor items depends on the facts. Security or glazing hazards should be reported as urgent.
impact: Record draughts, water entry, security incidents, unusable rooms and additional heating. Photographs should show the defect and its consequence, not merely condensation on the glass.
faqs: Are draughty windows automatically disrepair?
Not always. Significant gaps or failed components differ from the normal performance of older glazing and require factual assessment.
What if an external door does not lock?
Report the security risk urgently and retain the reference and any police or incident record.
Can higher heating bills be considered?
Potentially, where a clear defect and reliable bills or usage evidence support the additional cost.
